planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun; this winter-grower needs a wet winter-spring season followed by bone-dry summer dormancy.

directions: Bearded moraea gets its common name from the fine cilia (hair-like fringing) along its narrow leaf margins, a texture that distinguishes it from smoother-leaved relatives in the genus. A single fragrant flower opens per stem in winter to spring, with pale petals marked in blue, yellow, and brown tones that create a strikingly patterned bicolor or tricolor face. Like other Western Cape fynbos corms, it needs sharp drainage and full winter-spring moisture, followed by a completely dry summer rest while dormant underground. Grow it in a bulb frame or unheated greenhouse outside of true winter-rainfall climates to control the seasonal watering cycle.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; the species is widespread across varied Western Cape soils but still needs dry summer dormancy.

directions: Known in Afrikaans as bloutulp (blue tulip), this graceful corm sends up slender stems topped with pale to dark blue, purple, or violet flowers marked with triangular nectar guides near the base of each petal. It is one of the more widely distributed Moraea species in the Western Cape, tolerating a broader range of soil types than many of its rarer relatives, though it still follows the typical fynbos pattern of winter-spring growth and complete summer dormancy. Flowers open in late winter into spring and last only a day or two each, with new buds opening in succession. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, and withhold all water once the foliage yellows and dies back for summer.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; in wetter or colder climates, lift corms after bloom and store dry over summer rather than leaving them in the ground.

directions: This named selection of the South African flame freesia produces narrow fans of flattened, pleated leaves in fall followed by upright spikes of brilliant orange-red, six-parted flowers in mid-to-late spring, each blossom tubular at the base and widely flared above. It is noticeably more cold tolerant than many Cape corms, reportedly handling brief dips to around 15 degrees F, which makes it a workable garden plant in zone 8 as well as warmer zones. Flowers hold up exceptionally well when cut, making this cultivar a popular choice for cut-flower use in addition to rock garden and border plantings. Like the species, it wants dry summer dormancy and should not be kept wet once foliage dies back after bloom.

common_name: Page's Cone Plant (Lipped Fig-Shaped Mimicry Succulent)

planting.note: Grow in bright light with some shade from the hottest midday sun, in an extremely fast-draining mineral mix; this winter-grower must stay bone-dry through summer dormancy.

directions: Each body of this clustering Namaqualand mesemb is shaped like a small fig or inverted cone, formed from two fused, dull gray-green leaves that meet at a puckered, red-ringed fissure resembling a pair of lips. Colonies slowly build into dense mounds of these fig-like bodies over years of seasonal growth. Flowers emerge from the central fissure in late summer to early fall, typically in shades of yellow, pink, or purple, often opening in the afternoon. As with other winter-growing Conophytum, water only during the cool season and withhold water completely through the hot summer rest, when the outer leaf layer dries to a protective papery sheath.
sources: International Conophytum & Mesemb Study Group resources

planting.note: Grow in bright light with some protection from intense midday sun, in an extremely fast-draining mineral mix; keep completely dry through summer dormancy.

directions: True to its name, this species forms globose to inverted pear-shaped bodies that cluster densely into compact mounds resembling a bunch of small grapes or smooth pebbles. The grayish-green to reddish epidermis is often spotted or streaked, adding to its camouflaged, stone-like appearance among gravel in its Northern and Western Cape habitat. Pale yellow to white, often red-tipped flowers open at night in fall, giving off fragrance to attract nocturnal pollinators rather than putting on a showy daytime display. Provide the same winter-growing, summer-dormant care as other Conophytum, watering only during the cool season and keeping the mix bone dry once the plant shrinks back into its papery dormant sheath for summer.

planting.note: Grow in bright light with some protection from the hottest midday sun, in an extremely fast-draining mineral mix; keep bone dry through summer dormancy.

directions: One of the smallest species in an already diminutive genus, each smooth gray-green body of this North-Western Cape mesemb stands only about a third of an inch tall but offsets freely to form lax mats or ball-shaped mounds over time. Masses of bright pink to reddish-purple daisy-like flowers, occasionally white, open during the day in fall and are scentless, covering the clump in color far out of proportion to the plants' tiny size. It occurs naturally on rocky granite, shale, or quartz gravel flats around Namaqualand and the Vanrhynsdorp-Calvinia area, which explains its tolerance for extremely lean, sharply drained mixes in cultivation. Follow standard winter-growing Conophytum culture, watering only in the cool months and withholding water entirely during the hot summer rest.

planting.note: Pot in fall into a very sharply drained mineral mix with added limestone chips or coarse sand in full sun; this winter grower needs minimal water to avoid rot.

directions: Hugo's titanopsis forms a dense clustering clump of rosettes, each made up of several pairs of pale gray-blue to bluish-green leaves whose broad, warty tips carry a distinctive reddish tinge not found in the more uniformly gray-tipped Titanopsis calcarea. The rough, crystalline-textured leaf tips mimic weathered limestone outcrops in its native Northern Cape and Namibian habitat, giving effective camouflage against grazing animals. Yellow to salmon daisy-like flowers appear from among the leaf clusters in fall and winter. Grow it exactly as other Titanopsis species, in lean, sharply drained mineral soil in full sun, watering sparingly through the cool growing season and keeping it nearly dry during the hottest summer months.

planting.note: Pot in fall into a very sharply drained mineral mix with added limestone chips or coarse sand in full sun; water sparingly, as this winter grower is prone to rot if kept too wet.

directions: Fuller's titanopsis forms tight clumps of small rosettes, each with several pairs of blue-green, reddish-tinged leaves ending in a rounded triangular tip roughly an inch long, covered in rough tubercles that range from whitish or gray to ochre, red, or bluish depending on the individual plant. This tubercle coloring is more variable than in most other Titanopsis species, giving established clumps an unusually mottled, rock-like look. Yellow to amber daisy-like flowers open in fall and winter from among the rosettes. It is native to the Upper Karoo of South Africa and Bushmanland in Namibia, and like its relatives it needs the same lean, sharply drained mineral mix, full sun, and sparing winter-season watering, with an even drier rest through summer heat.
